overallSettings.studyTitle: Household Observation for Pandemic Preparedness and Emerging Respiratory Viruses Study
overallSettings.studyDescription:
Why have I been invited?
You have been invited to take part in this research study because seasonal respiratory viruses such as flu (influenza), Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), and human metapneumovirus (hMPV) and many others commonly circulate during the winter season.

This study aims to improve understanding of respiratory viruses, including how they spread within households, how the amount of virus changes over time and how infections affect individuals. To do this, we are inviting households in advance so we can collect information both before any illness occurs and also begin sampling quickly if an infection develops.

We will ask you to provide a number of different samples and some basic information about you and your household including whether or not you are experiencing any symptoms. Regardless of whether you become unwell during this study, your participation will help answer key public health questions.

Before you decide whether you want to participate, it is important that you understand why the research is being done and what the study will involve. Please take your time to read this information carefully and discuss it with others if you wish.

What is the purpose of the study?
The purpose of this study is to improve understanding of how seasonal respiratory viruses spread within households and how they affect people living together.

Households are helpful for this research because infections can pass easily between people in close contact, allowing us to follow how illness develops over time.

Although much is already known about these flu (influenza), Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), and human metapneumovirus (hMPV), they change over time. By collecting biological and environmental samples, along with some basic health information from you and your household, we aim to monitor currently circulating strains and update what is known about symptoms, how long people may be infectious, how easily infection spreads, and what factors affect the chance of becoming infected.

Do I have to take part?
No. Taking part in this study is entirely voluntary.

If you decide to take part, you will be asked to sign a consent form. You can also access this information sheet online at any time https://www.imperial.ac.uk/medicine/nihr-hpru-respiratory-infections/

Even after you agree to take part, you are free to withdraw at any time without giving a reason via the study app or, by contacting the study team by email at hopper-study@imperial.ac.uk. Choosing not to take part, or choosing to withdraw later, will not affect the standard of care you receive now or in the future.

Why have I been chosen?
You have been invited because you we are approaching the winter season when seasonal respiratory viruses are most common. We are inviting people who live in households of two or more members so we can study how these infections spread and affect people in the community.

What will happen to me if I agree to take part?
This is an observational study, which means we will collect health-related information, samples and symptom information from you. We will not give you any treatment or alter your usual medical care.

You will not need to visit a clinic. The study will take place entirely at your home. Everything you need to collect samples will be sent directly to your home. A courier will collect your samples and return them to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) or Imperial College London facilities.

More specific details of the enrolment process, and which samples to collect and when are given below. You will also be guided through each stage of the study using our study app, which provides access to all required forms and sends daily reminders for sample collection and other study activities.

Joining the study (enrolment):
If you decide to take part after reading the Participant Information Sheet (PIS) please follow the steps within the app to get started and enrol for the study.

Next you will be prompted to complete the following forms in the app:
1. Informed Consent Form (ICF): This allows you to indicate what you do and do not agree to, including whether you consent to providing samples and sharing data (such as access relevant GP records).
2. Baseline (B) Form: This collects information about your household setting and basic details about you, including your age and any health conditions.

Completing these forms should take no more than 15 minutes to complete.

What do I do next?
Please press next to continue to the study enrolment process.

subFields.helpText: Why are we asking for your age?
subFields.helpTextInfo:
We're asking your age because the immune system changes over time, which affects how people catch and respond to respiratory viruses.
Age also helps us understand who tends to get infected first and who might spread the virus in the community, perhaps even without knowing it

subFields.label: What sex were you registered with at birth?
subFields.sublabel: A question about gender identity will follow later.
subFields.helpText: Why are we asking about the sex you were registered with at birth?
subFields.helpTextInfo:
We’re asking about the sex you were registered with at birth because biological differences, (such as hormone levels, lung size, and body fat distribution), even from early development, can influence how the body responds to respiratory infections throughout life.


We recognise that not everyone identifies with the sex they were registered with at birth, which is why we also ask a separate question about gender identity

subFields.label: Is the gender you identify with the same as your sex registered at birth?
Please select the option that best describes your gender identity
subFields.helpText: Why did we select these catagories for gender?
subFields.helpTextInfo:
We based our gender identity options on responses to the 2021 Census in England and Wales.
Most people who said their gender differed from their sex at birth identified as trans or non-binary.
We’ve included these options, plus an ‘other’ category, to stay simple and inclusive

options.text: A different gender identity not listed here

subFields.label: How would you describe your ethnicity?
subFields.sublabel: We recognise that these ethnic groups do not represent how all people identify. You're encouraged to write in your ethnicity using your own words within the next question.
subFields.helpText: Why are we asking about your ethnicity?|Why did we select these ethnicity groups?
subFields.helpTextInfo:
Collecting ethnicity information helps us ensure that our study population is representative of the broader population.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, studies showed that some ethnic groups, such as Black and South Asian communities, were more likely to be hospitalised or experienced serious illness compared to others.
Understanding these patterns is important to help us find better ways to protect everyone|In England and Wales, there is an agreed list of ethnic groups you can use when asking for someone’s ethnicity.
 The groups are usually those used in the Census, which happens every 10 years.

You can read more about how these ethnic groups were chosen on: www.ethnicity-facts-figures.service.gov.uk/style-guide/ethnic-groups

People born in different countries may have had different vaccinations or exposures growing up.

regFields.helpTextInfo: We are asking about your height and weight so we can calculate your body mass index (BMI). In most people, BMI correlates to body fat, with the higher the number, the more body fat you may have, but it’s not accurate in some cases. BMI alone doesn’t diagnose health.

subFields.helpText: Why are we asking you about whether you carry out bodybuilding or professional athletic training?
subFields.helpTextInfo: We ask if you do bodybuilding or professional athletic training because some people have a higher body mass index (BMI) score due to increased muscle mass. This helps us understand your health more accurately and ensures we interpret your information in the right context. It’s simply a way for us to get a clearer picture, without making any assumptions about your body

This includes any conditions that:
• Have lasted (or are expected to last) 12 months or more
• Require regular medication, treatment, or medical check-ups
• May affect how your body responds to illness or infection

Examples include asthma and diagnosed depression.

This does not include:
• Temporary illnesses or injuries (like a cold, allergies to cat hair, hemorrhoids, a recent urinary tract infection (UTI) or a broken bone that's healing normally)
• Mild or short-term mental health difficulties that don't require ongoing treatment
• Conditions that have been fully treated and no longer affect you
